2    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
Import of Wheat  
†*121. SHRI MOTILAL VORA : †† 
SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUB LIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the quantity of wheat imported from foreign countries in the year 2006-07; 
(b) the names of States from which complaints have been received that wheat 
imported from foreign countries is not fit for consumption; 
(c) whether Central Government has got these complaints investigated and if so, the 
details thereof; and 
(d) whether it is a fact that the wheat imported from foreign countries has not been 
found fit for human consumption as per the samples tested by Maharashtra Government? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (d) A Stat ement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) In the year 2006-07,60,79,555 tons of wheat was imported into the country on 
private and Government accounts. 
(b) to (d) Complaints have been received from Maharasht ra State that some samples 
drawn and tested from godowns/Fair Price Shops were  not found meeting PFA 
Standards. After receipt of complaints from the Sta te Government, samples were jointly 
drawn from FCI godowns by State Government and FCI Officials. The samples were got 
tested and found to be conforming to PFA Standards.  The Government of Maharashtra 
has been advised to get the existing stock of impor ted wheat in State Government 
godowns and Fair Price Shops examined for quality a nd to ensure that only wheat 
conforming to specified quality standards are issue d through Fair Price Shops. Under the 
Public Distribution System (Control, Order, 2001, b efore the foodgrains are issued from 
FCI godowns, joint sampling is to be done by FCI an d State Government Officials to 
ensure that only good quality foodgrains are issued  for distribution through the Fair Price 
Shops. Further, the Government have also advised al l State Food Secretaries to ensure 
that during transportation and storage all precauti ons are taken to ensure that there is no 
deterioration in the quality of foodgrains till the y are distributed to the ration card 
holders. State Governments have also been advised t hat stocks available with State 
Government Agencies and Fair Price Shops should be regularly inspected to ensure that 
only foodgrains conforming to the quality specifica tions are distributed to ration card 
holders. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I congratulate the House for an excel lent debate yesterday. Q. No. 121.

SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: Sir, I would like to know from the hon.-Minister whether 
it is a fact that the Government after specifying c ertain standards have relaxed certain 
specifications for the wheat imported from Australi a and other places because there were 
widespread reports in the media in various parts of the country. 
Two, with regard to Maharashtra, the Human Rights Commission has gone into the issue 
and has said that this supplied material, food, is not fit for human consumption. Many samples 
were drawn and apanchanama was conducted and it was concluded that it was not fit for 
human consumption. What is the action taken; what is the quantum of it; how serious is the 
problem; and what are the steps taken by the hon. Minister in this regard? 

Oral Answers [23 NOV. 2007] to Questions   5 
 
 SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, I have already said that i n Maharashtra the total 
allocation was 13,97,000 tonnes. Complaints came from Bombay-Thane area and there is a 
district called Sindhudurg. Out of written complaints which we got, there are two types of 
complaints. One, a few individuals have collected some information from some shops. They 
claim, 'from some shops.' Whatever material they co llected was not collected from the 
godowns of the Food Corporation of India; that has been collected from other shops. There 
were some statements from shopkeepers also that tha t particular wheat, which had been 
given to them, was not for Public Distribution System; that was for open market. And there 
was a delay because of certain steps which the Stat e Government took for distribution. 
(Interruptions) It is a factual position. But still we have taken each and every item seriously.

†*122. SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: †† 
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the attention of Central Government has been drawn towards the 
irregularities in the distribution of ration in West Bengal;

(b) if so, the steps taken to check the same; and 
(c) if no steps have been taken, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
(SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. A number of media reports have been received mentioning irregularities 
in the distribution of ration commodities under TPDS in West Bengal. These reports have 
been sent to the State Government for getting inquiries conducted into them, taking necessary 
action and submitting reports on Action taken. Two reports have been received from the 
State Government. The State Government has reported initation of suitable action against 
concerned persons, including some staff of the Department of Food and Supplies, Government 
of West Bengal responsible for the irregularities. 
This issue has been taken up with the State Government for taking all necessary action to 
streamline functioning of TPDS in the State. The St ate Government has assured to take 
required action. 
SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir . I am happy that from the 
reply of the Government it is clear that the West B engal Government has finally admitted 
that there is irregularity at their end. 
Is it correct that a Central Minister from West Bengal sought the intervention of the hon. 
Agriculture Minister after violent trouble erupted in several districts of West Bengal? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, in fact, I want to request the hon. Chief Minister of the 
State that we should allot more for that particular State. Similar requests also came from one 
of my colleagues and additional allocation was made for festival purpose. 
SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: My second supplementary is this. Has the attention of the 
Government been drawn to the report that All India General Secretary of Fair Price Shop 
Dealers' Federation, who is leading the agitation against the West Bengal Government, has 
claimed patronage to two hon. CMP leaders of this House. They are not present now. Will 
the Government ensure that action is taken against him, notwithstanding the patronage that 
he enjoys? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, in fact, we have seen some Press reports including what 
the hon. Member has mentioned. We have sent every r eport to the State Government for 
inquiry and we are expecting a final reply from them. We got some replies on some of the 
issues where the Government of West Bengal has accepted that there are certain small mistakes 
and small irregularities, and they are taking corrective action. But the main demand of the 
State Government was that we should allot more for Above Poverty Line category. The 
Government of India has taken the entire responsbility for the AAY and Below Poverty Line 
Category. But, as for the APL category, it depends on the availability of stocks. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Bal Apte. (Interruptions)...  
SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: Sir, he has not answered my question. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Apte, please proceed. 
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Sir, is it a fact that the Centre has, in fact, given 
supply of wheat and rice, but the West Bengal Government has faled to lift them and, therefore,

there was scarcity and that scarcity has further enhanced because the cadres of the CPM, 
who are actually the dealers, did not distribute them? 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: Please authenticate it. (Interruptions).,.  
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: It is there on record that the CPM cadres  are 
distributors. (Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please (Interruptions)... Kindly allow the Question Hour to proceed. 
(Interruptions)...  
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: The Government is run by cadres. 
(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Will the please allow the Minister to answer the question? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, whatever complaint was received, we have referred to the 
State Government. The State Government has replied to some of the cases and communicated 
that they would like to take corrective action in regard to these cases. They have not mentioned 
anything regarding 'a' belongs to this cadre and 'b ' belongs to that cadre. This type of 
information is not there with the Government. But the second important question was asked 
about what was the allocation and actually how much was lifted. Sir, I have got the figures, 
for instance, from April, 2007 to September, 2007. The total allocation of rice to West 
Bengal was 6,52,788 tonnes and the offtake was 5,33,377 tonnes. 
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Not lifted! 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: In the case of rice, yes, there is a gap of 1,20,000 tonnes, 
(Interruptions)...  
SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Therefore, there is scarcity. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: The total allocation of wheat wa s 4,34,844 tonnes and the 
actual off take was 4,02,000 tonnes. In the case of  rice, there is a gap and we have 
communicated it to the State Government. Now we have stopped that.

Oral Answers [23 NOV. 2007] to Questions    13 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, I have to make one thing ve ry clear. Actually, the 
Government does not give money to the State. The Go vernment makes allocation for 
foodgrains which are subsidised foodgrains. The hon. Member is right that the subsidy come to Rs. 
23,000 to Rs.24,000 crores. There are no two opinions about it. And, as I said already to the 
House, after we got a report about this diversion, a number of actions have been taken and, 
definitely, there is an improvement. Still there are States where the Public Distribution System is 
not effectively implemented, and that is the reasons why meeting were called on the question of 
food security; the Food Ministers' meeting were also called. The hon. Member has suggested that we 
should request the hon. Prime Minister to call a me eting of the Chief Ministers. I have no 
objection to it. It is a very impportant subject. Substantial money has been provided for the sake 
of poor sections of the society. So, in order to ensure effective implementation of the scheme, I 
would request the hon. Prime Minister to call a meeting and discuss and bring it to the notice 
of all the Chief Ministers. 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Sir, our Government is ve ry much committed to 
strengthening the Public Distribution System for both the APL and BPL categories. But, so far as 
our information goes, there is a huge difference between the quantum of foodgrains requisitioned 
by the Government vis-a-vis the allocations made to the States. Now, I could not hear exactly the 
hon. Minister. So far as my information goes, as far as rice is concerned, 2.29 lakh tonnes till April 
was the quantum of allotment. Then, frorn May, it was reduced to 7700 tonnes. As far as wheat is 
concerned, the figure is 2.93 lakh tonnes. Then, in May, 2006, it was reduced to 9102 
tonnes; and, it was further reduced to 59,040 tonnes from June, 2007. So, when it was 2.93 lakh 
tonnes up to April, subsequently, it got reduced. So, my supplementary to the hon. Minister is 
whether we are committed towards strengthening the Public Distribution System. Considering the 
quantum of foodgrains requisitioned by the Government of India vis-a-vis the actual allotment 
during the last six months, how would the Governmen t of India actually fulfill the total 
requirement of the States so that the Public Distribution System is strengthened? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: As I have already explained to the hon. House regarding actual 
allotment and actual off-take, now, the information has been sought about the APL and the BPL 
categories. As for these categories, we have not changed the quantum, that is, whatever has been 
allotted for a number of years, and we are maintaining that. Of course, the figure mentioned by the 
hon. Member is correct. But I will be happy to give the figures of allocation of rice for APL 
categories and the actual off-take. In the month of April, 2007, the allocation was 7700 tonnes and 
the actual off-take was 5,662 tonnes. In May, 7700 tonnes were allocated and the actual lifting was 
14,753 tonnes. In June, 7700 tonnes were allocated, and the off-take was 6,638 tonnes. In July, 
the allocation was 7700 tonnes and 13,477 tonnes were lifted ...(Interruptions)  
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: Sir, we are not supposed to interrupt the hon. Minister. But 
there seems to be something wrong with the figures. He says, "allocation was 7700 tonnes and 
the off-take was 13.477 tonnes." 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: This is the case in respect of two years when because of festivals 
adequate quantity was given. But if you see the allocation and the actual off-take, practically, except 
two years, the off-take was less than the allocation in respect of APL categories. That is the 
factual position.

Public Distribution System was not properly handled. I would like to know from the

Conversion of Railway Stations as world class  
* 123. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal under active consideration of Government for conversion of 
railway stations as world class railway stations; 
(b) if so, the names of such stations, zone-wise; 
(c) whether Azamgarh Railway Station in Uttar Pradesh is also included in the list of world 
class railway stations; and 
(d) if not, the main reasons for such a discrimination with Azamgarh railway station? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Satement  
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Twenty two (22) stations as listed hereunder (Zone-wise) have been identified for 
development as World Class station:  
Railway No. of 
Stations 
Names of the Stations 
Central 2 Pune, CST Mumbai (Carnac Bunder) 
Eastern 1 Howrah 
Northern 7 Lucknow, New. Delhi, Anand Vihar, Bijwasan, Amritsar, Chandigarh & 
Varanasi 
Southern 2 Chennai & Thiruvananthapuram 
South Central 1 Secunderabad 
Western 1 Ahmedabad 
East Central 2 Patna & Gaya 
East Coast 1 Bhubaneshwar 
North Central 2 Mathura & Agra 
South Western 1 Bangalore 
West Central 1 Bhopal 
North Western 1 Jaipur 
TOTAL : 22  
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) The Government has decided to develop the identified stations of metros and mini metros 
and important tourist centres in first instance on the basis of need, potential viability and project 
implementation capacity.

Blind population in the country 
*124. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has become home to the world's largest number of blind 
people; 
(b) if so, how many eye donation banks are available in the country, particularly in 
Maharashtra State and how many of them donate eyes every year; 
(c) how many optometrists pass out every year and considering our population, whether 
they are sufficient to fulfil patients requirements; and 
(d) whether Government has set any target to eliminate blindness or control of blindness 
and if so, the details thereof? 
†[ ]Transliteration in Urdu Script.  

22    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions  
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) As per the World Health Organization estimates, out of total 37 million 
blind persons (Visual Acuity <3/60) in the world, 6.7 million are in India which is one-fifth 
of the total global blind population. 
(b) As per the Eye Bank Association of India, Hyderabad, there are 500 Eye Banks/Eye 
Donation Centres in the country including 148 in Maharashtra. Around 30,000 donated eyes 
are collected annually in the country. 
(c) There are about 6000 Optometrists in India and about 1200 pass out every year. More 
Optometrists are  needed to fulfill patients' requirements for eye care in the country as the 
Ophthalmologists—para medical personnel ratio shoul d be 1:4. 
(d) As per the survey conducted during 2006-07, the prevalence of Blindness in the country 
has come down to 1% as compared to 1.1% during the year 2001-02. 
The National Programme for Control of Blindness (NP CB) is committed to reduce the 
burden of avoidable blindness to 0.3% by the year 2020. 
The following steps have been taken under NPCB to achieve the targets and for effective 
implementation of the programme:— 
1. Setting up of State Blindness Control Societies and District Blindness Control Societies 
in States/UTs. 
2. Providing Eye care facilities to the needy people at Primary, Secondary and Tertiary levels 
through Primary Health Centres, District Hospitals, Medical Colleges and Regional 
Institutes of Ophthalmology. 
3. Strengthening of Eye Banks in Government/Voluntary Sector. 
4. Financial support to NGOs for strengthening their existing infrastructure for Eye care and 
providing recurring grant for Cataract surgery, School Eye Screening and Eye Donation. 
5. Organizing Eye Donation Fortnight from 25th August to 8th September every year to 
promote eye donation. 
6. Screening of School Children for detection of refractive errors and providing free spectacles 
to poor children. 
7. Strengthening of Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology/eye departments of Medical 
Colleges by providing assistance for development of paediatric eye units/low vision units/ 
retina units and training infrastructure. 
8. Imparting training to Ophthalmic Surgeons from Government Hospitals/Medical Colleges 
for quality eye care. 
9. Intensification of IEC activities Jo create awareness about eye care activities.

Contract Farming 
*127. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of cases of contract farming in operation and cases of corporate farming 
in Maharashtra; and 
(b) what are the steps taken to set up a strong system to monitor contracts, so as to avoid 
exploitation of the workers/growers/farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) The State 
Government of Maharashtra has informed that no case s of contract farming have been 
registered in the State so far under the provision of Contract Farming introduced with effect 
from 11th July, 2006 by amending the Maharashtra St ate Agricultural Produce Marketing 
(Regulation) Act, 1963. Since corporate farming does not come in the purview of Maharashtra 
State Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1963 and it is not being promoted 
under the contract farming arrangements, no information is being maintained by the State 
Government in this regard. 

26    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions  
(b) Under the provisions of Contract Farming in the Maharashtra State Agricultural Produce 
Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1963, various terms and  conditions, which are to be adhered 
while entering into Contract Farming Agreements, are as under: 
1. Contract Farming Sponsor shall register himself with the Market Committee or with the 
prescribed officer, in such manner as prescribed under the Rules. 
2. The Contract Fanning Sponsor shall get the Contract Farming Agreement recorded with the 
officer prescribed in this behalf. The Contract Farming agreement shall be in such form, 
containing such particulars and terms and conditions, as may be prescribed. 
3. Notwithstanding anything contained in the Contract Farming Agreement or the Indian Contract 
Act, 1872 or any other law for the time being in force, no title, or rights in or ownership or 
possession of agricultural land of the Contract Farming Producer shall be transferred, alienated 
or vested in the Contract Farming Sponsor or his successor or his agent. 
4. Dispute arising out of any Contract Farming Agreement may be referred to a settlement authority 
as may be prescribed in this behalf. The settlement authority shall resolve the dispute in a 
summary manner within thirty days, after giving the parties a reasonable opportunity of being 
heard. 
5. The party aggrieved by the decision of the settlement authority may prefer an appeal to the 
Appellate Authority as may be prescribed in this behalf, within thirty days from the date of the 
decision. The appellate Authority shall dispose of the appeal within thirty days, after giving the 
parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard and the decision of the Appellate Authority 
shall be final. 
6. The decision of the settlement authority and the decision of the Appellate Authority in appeal 
shall have force of the decree of a Civil Court and shall be enforceable as such and the decretal 
amount shall be recovered as an arrears of land revenue. 
7. Dispute relating to and arising out of a Contract Farming Agreement shall not be called in 
question in any court of law. 
8. The agricultural produce covered under the Contract Farming Agreement may be sold to the 
Contract Farming Sponsor outside the market yard and in such a case, no market fee shall be 
leviable. 
Under the Maharashtra State Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Rules, 1967, 
provisions regarding registration of Sponsor with the District Deputy Registrar (DDR), Co-
operative Society have been made compulsory, and this registration will be for one year only. 
The original copy of Contract Fanning Agreement will have to be submitted to the DDR, Co-
operative Societies and the Sponsor shall be liable  to pay cost of supervision to the State 
Government. The Sponsor is prohibited from raising any permanent infrastructure or creating any 
lease hold rights or charge on the land of the farmers/producers, recovery of loans and advances 
given to the farmers/producers can be recovered only from the agricultural produce and in no case 
sale of the land will be allowed, the minimum period of agreement shall be for once crop season 
and maximum period shall not be more than 3 years. Along with this a model draft of the 
Agreement to be entered into between the sponsor and farmers/ producers has also been prescribed. 
Thus, through these provisions, a strong system has been set up in the State to monitor the 
contracts so as to avoid exploitation of the workers/ growers/farmers.

Food riots against PDS agents in West Bengal 
*128. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware of food riots against P DS agents that took place in 
certain districts of West Bengal; 
(b) if so, the details of causes; 
(c) whether Government has taken up the issue with the State Government; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to discount such incidents by improving efficacy of PDS? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
(SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) As per reports received from the State Government 
of West Bengal, there have not been any food riots in the State. However, agitation against 
Fair Price Shop (FPS) dealers has taken place in Bi rbhum, Burdwan, Bankura and 
Murshidabad districts in the State. The main reason mentioned by the State Government for 
the agitation against the FPS dealers is improper distribution of wheat to the APL Cardholders 
by the FPS dealers. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Government has taken up the issue with the State Government. 
Various reports/complaints received about irregularities in functioning of TPDS in the State 
have been sent to State Government for inquiry, app ropriate action and report to the 
Government of India on the action taken. The State Government has assured to take necessary 
action against all those responsible for irregularities in functioning of TPDS and to streamline 
functioning of the TPDS in the State.

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
(SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (d) A tender was floated by the State Trading Corporation 
(STC) for import of 10 lakh tons of wheat on 30th April, 2007. The STC recommended 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

38    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions  
purchase of 3.06 lakh tons of wheat at a weighted average price of US $ 263 per ton. However, 
STC advised that there were possibilities of softening of prices for arrival beyond August, 
2007 as compared to the prices received in the tender for the following reasons: 
(i) Fresh crop is due for harvest in July/August, 2007 in exporting countries like Russia, France, 
Germany, Ukraine, etc. 
(ii) The Australian crop to be harvested during November/December, 2007 is reported to be good 
as per the IGC report of April, 2007 which may have a softening effect on wheat prices. 
(iii) The prices quoted by suppliers for June/July, 2007 delivery is higher than for July/August 
delivery, indicating lower prices in subsequent months. 
The IGC report dated 24.5.2007 showed that prices were declining from the beginning of 
May upto 23rd of May. Further, domestic wheat procurement was still going on and it was 
apprehended that import of wheat at a higher price would induce hoarding of wheat stocks in 
the hope of future price rise thereby adversely affecting procurement. The CBOT futures did 
not show any indication of spurt in prices in the n ear future. Therefor, the Government 
decided not to purchase wheat at US $ 263 per ton. 
On June 11, 2007 the global estimate of wheat produ ction was downgraded from more 
than 621 million tons to 610 million tons by USDA a nd soon after by the International 
Grains Council (IGC). Thereafter, the CBOT futures and spot prices of wheat started 
increasing in the international market. The domestic procurement was only about 110 lakh 
tons as against estimated requirement of 150 lakh t ons of wheat required for the Central 
Pool. After assessing the requirements of food security and international prices of wheat, it 
was decided to float a tender to import one million tons of wheat. Accordingly, STC invited 
tenders on 26.6.2007 and recommended the purchase o f 5.11 lakh tons of wheat at US $ 
325.59 Per ton. The STC had taken into account all relevant information and also consulted 
experts in the field before making the recommendation. The ocean freight had also gone up 
considerably. The CBOT futures were showing a bullish trend pointing to higher prices in 
the international market in the coming months. Based on these, the Government decided to 
purchase 5.11 lakh tons of wheat at US $ 325.59 per ton. 
The Government reviewed the position of buffer stocks and decided to float a tender in 
August for purchase of wheat. As against the buffer stock norms of 171 lakh tons on 1st July, 
2007, the actual stock was 129 lakh tons. The CBOT futures were showing a bullish trend in 
the coming months. There were reports of major wheat producing countries placing restrictions 
on wheat imports. 'The tender was opened on 29.8.2007. The STC recommended pruchase 
of 7.95 lakh tons of wheat at a weighted average pr ice of US $ 389.45 per ton, which was 
accepted by the Government. 
The import of wheat was done by the Government taking into account the requirements 
of food security, the need for maintaining buffer stocks as per norms to meet the requirements 
of the Public Distribution System, Welfare Schemes, natural calamities, etc., the domestic 
wheat procurement, international spot and futures p rices and estimates of global wheat 
production at the relevant time. The estimates of global production are done by International 
Grains Council (IGC) and US Department of Agriculture (USDA). The estimates made by 
them are published every month. Government of India  has no independent agency for 
estimating global production.

Level of alkalinity in soil/fertile tend  
533. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that due to continuous and increased use of chemical fertilizers, the level 
of alkalinity and salinity in the soil/fertile land has gone up high; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that the use of gypsum has been very useful in brining down 
salinity and alkalinity level; and 
(c) if so, the immediate efforts being made by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI LAL 
BHURIA): (a) There is no evidence to suggest about increased level of alkalinity and salinity in 
the soil due to continuous and increased use of chemical fertilizers. Investigations under All India 
Coordinated Research Project under Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) on 'Long Term 
Fertilizer Experiments' over the last few decades in different locations also didn't reveal such 
instances. 
(b) and (c) Gypsum is being used for recalmation of  alkaline soils. The Government is 
implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Reclamation of Alkali Soil (RAS) since 7th 
Five Year Plan for reclamation of soils, which are suffering from alkalinity. Presently this scheme 
is subsumed under Macro Management of Agriculture (MMA). Under the scheme, financial 
assistance limited to 25% is being given for providing soil amendment (Gypsum/ pyrite) @ 50% 
of Gypsum Required value or maximum of 5 tonnes per hectare for isolated approach and 
maximum of 15 tonnes per hectare for projectized approach. 
Policy on contract farming  
534. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is actively considering to frame a policy on contract farming with a 
view to co-ordinate production and marketing activities; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and when it is expected to be initiated; and 
(c) how far this shall be helpful to the small farmers for better remuneration of their produce 
particularly in backward areas/districts of Uttar Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI LAL 
BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Model Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act circulated by 
the Central Government to the States in 2003 for implementing marketing reforms has provisions 
for the registration of contract farming sponsors and recording of contract farming agreements 
with the Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee (APMC) or a prescribed authority under the 
Act, protection of title or rights of the farmers o ver the land under such cotnracts, dispute 
settlement mechanism and a model draft agreement suggesting various terms and conditions. To 
help States in the formulation of Rules in this reg ard, the Ministry of Agriculture has also 
circulated a set of Model APMC Rules to them for adoption. By now, relevant provisions have 
been made by several State Governments/ UTs in their respective APMC Acts for providing a legal 
framework to contract farming. In seven States/Union Territories there are no APMC Acts, 
therefore, there is no regulation of contract farming in such States/UTs. The Model Act circulated 
by the Ministry is suggestive in nature, and, since Agriculture is a State subject, it is for the State 
Governments to decide on the implementation, intermediation and monitoring of the contract 
farming arrangements in their State.

(c) The legal framework for contract farming under the State Agricultural Produce 
Marketing (Regulation) Acts will be quite helpful t o the small farmers in securing better 
remuneration for their produce, particularly in bac kward areas/districts, including that of 
Uttar Pradesh, as, such arrangements would cover th e price risk and also the production 
risk to a great extent. Contract Farming has the po tential of combining small farmers' 
efficiency with economy of scale, utilizing corporate management skills, providing assured 
markets and reducing transaction costs in the value chain by ensuring vertical integration. 
Several national and multinational processors of fast food chains are increasingly entering 
into contract with the farmers to encourage them to cultivate farm products (fruit, vegetables, 
etc.) of the desired quality by providing them not only seeds and other inputs but also 
assured procurement of the produce at pre-decided p rices. Such tie-ups have special 
significance for small and marginal farmers, who have small marketed surplus and do not 
have staying power. They may not individually be capable of investing in technology, but 
through self help groups or cooperatives, there cou ld emerge a desirable institutional 
framework, through which farmers can suitably reap the benefits of contract farming 
arrangements. Contract farming is particularly useful for high value crops because it enables 
the corporates to associate with the farmers and helps in imparting the latest technological 
know how to them.

The Working Group of the Sub-Committee of the Natio nal Development Council

Apart from above watershed development related sche mes, Government of India have 
also initiated two major centrally sponsored schemes to benefit rainfed areas. 
(a) National Horticulture Mission: The scheme is for de velopment of horticulture duly 
ensuring end to end approach having backward and fo rward linkages covering research, 
production, post harvest management, processing and  marketing. Provisional outlay of 
Rs. 8809 crores has been made for the XI Plan. 
(b) Micro Irrigation: The scheme aims at judisious use of water resource by adopting 
efficient methods of application to save water and to increase water use efficiency. Provisional 
outlay of Rs. 3500 crores has been made for the XI Plan. 
The Government has also taken new initiatives for improving agricultural production in 
the XI Five Year Plan by launching of new programmes. The important ones are:— 
1. National Food Security Mission —This Mission has been launched with the objective 
to enhance the production of rice, wheat and pulses by 10,8 and 2 million tonnes respectively 
by the end of XI five year plan. It is being implemented in 16 States. Provisional outlay of 
Rs. 4883 crores has been made for the XI Plan.  
2. Rastriya Krishi Vikash Yojana — This scheme has been launched to incentivize the 
States to increase the share of agriculture to the State Plans. The scheme aims at achieving 
4% annual growth in agriculture sector during XI plan by ensuring a holistic development of 
agriculture and allied sectors. The scheme will be implemented based on the State and District 
Agricultural Plans suitable to the respective agro-climatic conditions. The funds are being 
provided to the States as additional central assist ance as 100% grant by the Central 
Government. Under the scheme, the States have the freedom to develop and pursue activities 
on the basis of their priorities through State and District Agricultural Plans. An outlay of 
Rs. 25000 crores has been provided for the XI Plan. 
3. National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA) — To address the problems of farmers of 
rainfed areas, for bringing effective coordination,  convergence and to provide the much-
needed knowledge inputs regarding systematic up-gradation and management of country's 
dryland and rainfed agriculture, Government of India has set up the National Rainfed Area 
Authority (NRAA). This Authority is a two-tier stru cture. The first tier is the Governing 
Board chaired by the union Minister of Agriculture, whereas Minister, Rural Development 
is the Co-Chairman and the Ministers of Environment & Forests and Water Resources are 
the Members. The second tier Is the Executive Committee with Technical Experts, Subject 
Matter Specialists and the representatives of Stake Holder Minsitries as its Members, it is 
headed by the Chief Executive Officer of the NRAA. The Authority is an advisory, policy 
making and monitoring body mandated to prepare the perspective plan, outlining the National 
strategy and road map for holistic and sustainable development of rainfed farming areas. A 
Rainfed Area Development Programme has been planned for the XI Five year Plan with an 
outlay of Rs. 2500 crores.

545. SHRI O.T. LEPCHA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has formulated any National Agriculture Policy for farmers to 
save them from drought/floods, etc., in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI 
LAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) In the event of natural calamities, such as, drought/flood, relief is 
provided under Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) and the National Calamity Contingency Fund. 
Calamity Relief Fund is a fund available with the S tate Government to provide immediate 
relief. For the year 2007-08, allocation of Rs. 425 8.85 crore is available out of which the 
share of Central Government is Rs. 3194.14 crore. F or severe natural calamities where the 
relief expenditure cannot be accommodated within th e CRF, additional funding from the 
Central Government is provided under the National Calamity Contingency Fund. Under the 
existing norms, assistance towards agricultural inp uts subsidy is admissible to small and 
marginal farmers where crop loss on account of natural calamities is 50% and above. Input 
subsidy is also admissible to farmers other than sm all and marginal farmers, in case of 
severe calamity occurring for a second consecutive year or subsequent year. Besides, Reserve 
Bank of India has issued guidelines to Banks for conversion/rescheduling of loans of farmers 
in the event of natural calamity. The national Agri culture Insurance Scheme is also under 
implementation with the objective to protect the fa rmers against crop losses suffered on 
account of natural calamities, such as drought, flood, hailstorm, cyclone, pests and diseases.

(a) whether it is a fact that there has been steep rise  in prices of essential foodgrains 
cereals and vegetables during this year;

(d) the steps taken by Government to make essential commodities available at affordable

pulses manily tur dal, has shown an upward trend. Retail prices of gram dal have reduced.

peak of Rs. 16 per kg in Delhi, reduced to 13 per kg and onion from Rs. 27 per kg has been

Wadhwa Committee on corruption in PDS  
574. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court had appointed Justice Wadhwa Committee to go into the 
problems ailing the country's PDS; 
(b) whether the Committee has submitted its report and if so, the details thereof and the 
action taken thereon; 

88    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
(c) whether the people of West Bengal have been agitating for corruption in PDS and if 
so, the reaction of the State/Central Government thereon; and 
(d) whether card holders in Delhi are not getting wheat and rice on their ration cards and 
if so, the action taken by Government to check the black-marketing of rationed items in 
Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Committee has submitted report relating to Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) in Delhi. Main recommendations of the Committee are abolition of APL category, 
identification of BPL & AAY families to check exclu sion, elimination of bogus cards, 
strengthening of Vigilance/enforcement Wing and Anti Hoarding Cell, computerization of 
PDS operations, establishment of Helpline, introduction of E-banking, distribution of wheat 
flour on option creation of independent agency to m onitor TPDS, introduction of food 
coupons, streamlining of FPS licensees and payment of reasonable commission to them, 
increasing awareness among the beneficiaries about the scheme, introduction of Global 
Positioning System (GPS) for movement of foodgrains  consignments, etc. The report has 
been sent to Government of NCT of Delhi for comments. 
(c) Report have been received about agitation against Fair Price Shops (FPSs) dealers in 
some parts of West Bengal due to improper distribut ion of foodgrains by them to Above 
Poverty Line (APL) cardholders. The Reports/complaints have been sent to the Government 
of West Bengal for inquiry and corrective measures. 
(d) The Government of NCT of Delhi has reported that card holders in Delhi are getting 
rice and wheat on their ration cards. It has also r eported that some complaints of black-
marketing of ration items have been received. To check black-marketing of ration items, the 
State Government has reported that— 
(i)   daily lifting of the Specified Food Articles (SFAs) is being monitored by the 
Department and DSCSC Ltd.; 
(ii)   information on lifting of SFAs is made available on website of the State Government 
for general public; 
(iii) Fair Price Shop Owners are to report arrival of SFAs to the Food Supply Officer 
in writing within 3 hours of receipt of the stock indicating quantity and time; 
(iv) Area Inspector is to visit and inspect the FPS  within 3 hours of receipt of 
information and record his visit in the receipt column of the Register; 
(v) officers of the Department would conduct monthl y random inspection of FPSs/ 
KODs; 
(vi) in case of minor variations of stock and overc harging, penalties have been 
prescribed; and 
(vii) a Special Task Force has been constituted to carry out inspections of PDS outlets 
to check quality and availability of stock under su pervision of Deputy 
Commissioner (Revenue)/SDM of the districts.

582.  PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Indian and USA have signed an agreement to collaborate on medical research 
aimed at developing low-cost diagnostic and therapeutic technologies for a range of diseases 
and would enable the two countries to undertake joint biomedical research towards developing 
better tools to treat diseases like malaria, tuberculosis and HIV; 
(b) if so, what are the other main features of the agreement; 
(c) by what time, the agreement is likely to be implemented; and 
(d) to what extent, it has been helpful for both the countries? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) Joint Statement between the Indian Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR) and U.S. Centres of Disease Control and Prev ention of the U.S. Deptt, of Health 
and Human Services was signed in Washington DC on June 7, 2005. The silent features of 
the agreement are as under: 
• Building of capacity including sharing of expertise  in the operation of high 
containment laboratories and safe handling of high hazard viruses and bacteria, 
development of protocols and standard operating procedures, collaborate and share 
expertise in the areas of epidemiological design, d iagnosis, vaccinology, 
immunology, hematology and molecular virology. 
• Developing, as well as refining, of repositories with more detailed characterization 
of strains stored in them, exchange of diagnostic r eagents, protocols, equipment, 
quality assurance, reliability of laboratory results and flow of information. 
• Strengthening capacity to identify new pathogens during outbreaks, including field 
investigation strategies, collaboration and training of staff in ICMR laboratories and 
at HHS/CDC, establishment of partnership between laboratory response and field 
epidemiology teams, analysis of pathological material during outbreaks of unknown 
etiology and development of diagnostic reagents for newly discovered agents. 
The implementation Plan between the The National In stitute of Allergy and Infections 
Diseases of the National Institute of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and 
the ICMR relating to expansion of Indo-US cooperation on emerging and re-emerging infectious 
diseases and disease surveillance was signed on 16th October, 2007. ICMR currently is in 
process to initiate various activities under the plan indicated. The activities involved in the 
agreed plan relate to research work, which is an on-going process, therefore, the time schedule 
for implementation of plan can not be indicated at this stage. However, it is envisaged that this 
partnership will increase joint activities in scientific discovery, research innovation and reinforce 
existing research cooperation, scientific training and capacity development efforts.

†586. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of HEAL TH AND FAMILY

for treatment in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that due to lack of adequate salary and proper facilities, most of the 
doctors are leaving Government institutes and joini ng private institutes and big private 
hospitals; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Government to stop this practice? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) As per information available, there are a total 4745 posts sanctioned 
in the Central Health Service, out of which 3491 po sts were filled up as on 1.1.2007. In 
respect of State Governments, as per the National H ealth Policy profile 2006 brought out 
by the Central Health Intelligence, there are 73549  allopathic doctors. Additionally, 
under NRHM there are 3673 doctors and 3163 speciali sts are working on contractual

(b) and (c) The Central Government had noted the increasing trend of Government doctors 
especially the Specialist seeking Voluntary Retirem ent or Resigning due to the attractive 
financial compensation and other generous service benefits in foreign assignments/domestic 
private sector. The Government had constituted and Expert Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Shri Javid Choudhury, Former Secret ary (Health) to suggest measures/ 
disincentives that should be introduced to arrest the outflow of doctors and changes in the 
terms and condition of service. The Committee has made a number of recommendations to 
improve the lot of these doctors. Amongst the steps  taken by Government (i) the age of 
retirement of specialists in three sub-cadres of Te aching, Non-teaching and Public Health

increased from two years to three years in respect of CHS doctors.

lakh deaths. Every month more than 1.0 lakh patient s are placed on DOTS. In 2006 
alone, India placed around 14.00 lakhs cases on DOT S, more than any country in a 
single year in the world. Overall performance of RN TCP has been excellent with cure/ 
treatment completion rate consistently above 85% an d death rate reduced to less than 
5%. To increase accessibility of the masses to the facilities provided under the

Banned drugs in circulation 
593. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in a bid to contain the growing divide between safe and banned drugs, which 
continue to be available over the counter inmost medical stores across the country, his Ministry 
has appointed a sub-committee to check into the circulation of banned drugs in the country; 
(b) if so, whether many drugs that are banned in other countries continue to be sold in our 
country; 
(c) to what extent, setting up of panel has helped in c hecking the circulation of banned 
drugs; and 
(d) what are the other concrete steps and measures cons idered to check sale of such 
banned drugs in future? 

108    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions  
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) Drugs, for which harmful effects or inadequate thereapeutic justification 
is reported in the context of current medical evide nce, are examined by Drugs Technical 
Advisory Board (DTAB) on a continuous basis. Drugs are banned in the country under 
Section 26A of Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Based on recommendations of DTAB, if a drug is 
found to be harmful, it is banned with immediate ef fect. If there is lack of therapeutic 
reationale, the drug is banned in a phase wise manner. 
(b) to (d) Every country has its own regulatory sys tem for approving or banning drugs 
after examining overall benefit rise ratio of the d rug in consultation with experts and is 
requirement in the country. The safety and efficacy of a drug is ascertained as per Schedule 
Y of Drugs and Consmetics Rules before market approval in the country. There is regulatory 
system in place for ensuring safety and efficacy of  drugs before market approval in the 
country. 
Examination of marketed drugs by DTAB is a continuo us process and based on the 
recommendations of DTAB, so far, 78 drugs/drug form ulations have been prohibited for 
marketing in the country. Sale of banned drugs in the country is a punishable offence under 
Section 28B of Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

competitive edge of MSMEs (both domestically and gl obally) have put in place several

improved infrastructure, better availability of cre dit, facilities for training and capacity

charges payable to Indian Railway Finance Corporation carried out in 2005-06 has approval of 
Comptroller & Auditor General of India. As regards accountal of reimbursement of loss on

Lease of iron ore mines 
622. SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: 
SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL), the owner of Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, has 
been applying for lease of iron ore mines for its captive use for several years; 
(b) if so, the steps have been taken to ensure such a captive iron ore mining right to RINL; and 
(c) whether his Ministry has recommended leasing of suc h mines to RINL to the 
Governments of different States where iron ore reserves are located, like Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, 
Orissa and Andhra Pradesh, etc.?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. AKHILESH DAS): (a) to (c) 
Yes, Sir. Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd., has applied for lease of iron ore mines in the States of Orissa, 
Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh. The applications made by RINL have been recommended by the 
Ministry of Steel to State Governments like Andhra Pradesh and to the Ministry of Mines. 
Set up of three greenfield pellet plants 
623. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether country's largest steel producer the Steel Authority of India Limited plans to set up 
three greenfield pellet plants with a total capacity of six million tonne and is likely to invest a sum of 
Rs. 1,000 crores for these projects; 

126   Papers Laid [RAJYA SABHA] on the Table  
(b) whether Government plans to review the progress of various steel projects and an 
inter-ministerial groups has set to review the progress of all major proposed plants; 
(c) whether many of the proposed plants are not making any progress due to problems in 
land acquisitions and iron ore mines; and 
(d) what concrete steps Government has taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. AKHILESH DAS): 
(a) Yes, Sir. Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) is planning to set up three new greenfield 
pellet plants. A plant of 0.9 Million tonnes per year capacity at Dalli mines in Chhattisgarh 
and a plant of around 1 Million tonnes per year cap acity at Gua mines in Jharkhand are 
being planned. There will no investment by SAIL for setting up these two plants. SAIL will 
provide iron ore fines to the parties who will set up the pellet plants and the parties will 
supply pellets to SAIL on 'conversion cost' basis. 
It has also been planned to set up another plant of 2 Million tonnes per year capacity at 
Taldih mines in Orissa for which the total investment will be made by SAIL. The process for 
engagement of consultant has been initiated. The cost of setting up the pellet plant would be 
known after finalization of the Detailed Project Report. 
(b) Yes, Sir. An Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) under the Chairmanship of Secrtary (Steel) 
and comprising Secretaries of the concerned Ministries and the Chief Secretaries of the concerned 
State Governments has been set up to monitor and coordinate various issues concerning major 
steel investments in the country. 
(c) and (d) Issues relating to land acquisition and iron ore linkages are key factors to be 
settled before various investment proposals of new steel projects progress. The - Inter 
Ministerial Group (IMG) will also be addressing some of these key issues confronting fresh 
steel investment proposals. The Ministry co-ordinates and recommends. Land acquisition is 
done by the State Government. Government of India h as also declared a new National 
Rehabilitation & Resettlement Policy 2007, which is expected to ease problems relating to 
the acquisition of land for such plants.

SHRI SHIVRAJ V PATIL: The point I am making is that  the framers of the Constitution 
have provided article 355 and article 356 with an intention of allowing the Union Government to 
take appropriate action in certain situations, but these articles have to be used very-very 
carefully. Mistakes can be committeed and then, we can cite the instances as to when the 
mistakes were committed - when nine State Governmen ts were dissolved; when in nine 
States, President's Rule was imposed. We are not re ferring to those instances. But, while 
discussing this issue, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar had s aid, "I hope that there will arise no 
occasions to make use of this article." And, what did he say? He said, "You do it in a very 
careful manner; when it is absolutely necessary." I  can assure this House, apart from the 
mistakes committed in the past by that Government, or some other Government, or someone 
else, or by ourselves, we would be very careful in using these articles. We would not say that 
when occasion arises, it would not be used, but we will not use it lightly or we will not use it in 
a manner which will be suspicious, which will not be acceptable to those who understand the 
provisions of the Constitution. I cannot say more than this. It is not necessary. 
I would like to congratulate Shrimati Sushma Swaraj. She presented the case in a propoer 
manner and I would like to say that all other Members also presented the case in a proper 
manner. Shrimati Brinda Karat, as usual, in her eloquent style, put the facts on behalf of her 
party in a very-very appropriate manner and I thank all the hon. Members who participated 
in this debate and made excellent contribution. Thank you, Sir.

Concern over malnutrition in children in the country 
 
MS. MABEL REBELLO. (Jharkhand): Sir, the recent report of UNICEF's Progress for Children, a 
report card on nutrition, relased globally on 4th May, indicates that India has the highest number of 
malnourished children in the world, with Madhya Pradesh being the worst affected State. 
 
About 47 per cent of under-fives, numbering 57 million children are underweight. Even in Sub-
Saharan Africa only 33 per cent of the children are malnourished. 
 
The worst affected States in India are Jharkhand, U P, Rajasthan, Orissa, Bihar and 
Maharashtra. Over SO per cent children in these States are malnourished. The reasons for 
India's pitiable performance are poor food quality,  low social status of women and early 
marriage, leading to low birth weight, bad quality hygiene and high rate of illiter

While releasing the report, UNICEF's India Chief Mr . Werner Schultink said, "No other 
country was worse off than India in case of malnour ished children. The causes for this are 
many—bad quality feeding, population density, high prevalance of infectious deseases, high 
rate of illiteracy among women, high prevalence of gender inequality, low rate of immunization and 
high rate-of birth of underweight babies. 
We must ensure that mothers feed newborn on breast milk, at leasts for six months from 
birth, reduce infectious diseases, especially diarrhoea and malaria, and counsel mothers on 
better infant care. 
This comes to request the Government to empower fam ilies by providing them with the 
resources and devices they need to improve health, feeding and childcare practices, and 
integrate child health and nutritional needs into national policy.

Concern over indo-asean trade agreement (posing a threat to the nation)  
SHRI P.R. RAJAN (Kerala): Sir, the Union Commerce Ministry has already declared that the 
discussion on free trade between India and ASEAN is complete and it is likely to be declared at any 
time. If the agreement is implemented, Kerala's agriculture sector will head to a severe crisis. It will 
affect pepper, tea, coffee, etc., as these items have been included in the Negative List of 490 
items in the agreement. India has also agreed to consider phase-by-phase reduction in import 
duties of these items, including palm oil. Reduction of import duty on palm oil will affect the coconut 
farmers of Kerala very adversely. Even now, because of import of pepper from Sri Lanka, Kerala's 
pepper farmers are facing severe crisis. If rubber is imported from Thailand and coconut from 
Vietnam, the fanners of keraia will be thrown to a difficult situation. 
Reducing the import duty on the agricultural products will be a set back not only for the farmers 
in Kerala, but also to the entire country. It has to be noted here that about 260 million people, 
who live below the poverty line, are entirely dependent on farming and related works and such 
decisions will make their life worse. 
The developing countries have realized that by agreeing to the Free Trade Agreement, they 
will lose their food security and sovereign rights on agricultural products. 
The food security of the country will be threatened by this decision. For the sake of farmers, I 
urge upon the Government to resist pressure from developed countries.

Demand for approval of allotment of coal blocks to Maharashtra State Mining  
Corporation  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE (Maharashtra): Sir, the Mahar ashtra Government had 
submitted a request to the Government of India for allotment of coal blocks to Maharashtra 
State Mining Corporation on 22nd August, 2002, to m ake up the wide gap between the 
demand and supply of electricity and coal. The prop osal is to reserve 27 coal blocks for 
mining for the Maharashtra State Mining Corporation . The matter was taken up by the 
Maharashtra Government with the Secretaries of Indu stry, Energy and Labour 
Departments, vide letter dated 22nd August, 2002,18th January, 2003,4 th February, 
2003,23rd November, 2004 and 10th January, 2006. In  spite of these reminders, the 
Central Government neither raised any points nor so ught any informtion from the 
Maharashtra Government. However, the Government of India vide its letter dated 2nd 
August, 2005, conveyed 'in principle' approval for working of Marki Zari Jamani, Adkoli 
Coal Block to MSMC and Gare Palama Sector-II Coal B lock to Tamil Nadu State 
Electricity Board and MSMC jointly. 
Sir, the approval for the remaining coal blocks is still awaited. In spite of several reminders 
from the Maharashtra Government, approval of coal blocks has not been granted so far. Sir, 
this matter is of great importance because demand and supply of electricity and coal is very 
much needed in the State of Maharashtra. If these p roposals are approved, it will help to 
great extent the Maharashtra Government. I, therefore, urge upon the Government to kindly 
approve the remaining coal blocks for Maharashtra at an early date.

PRIVATE MEMBER’S BUSINESS (RESOLUTIONS) 
Constitution of a committee for recommending amendments to constitution                      
for adding a new chapter on governance of coalition governments 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, I beg to move the following Resolution: 
"Having regard to the facts that— 
(i) an era of coalition governments at the national and States has crept in; 
(ii) Indian political scenario is not likely to change substantially in this respect in near future; 
(iii) there is no mechanism at present which can effectively find solutions to the problems which 
arise out of coalition form of Government; and 
(iv) there is a need to ensure that the nation does not suffer on account of delays, 
uncertainties under such dispensations; 
this House resolves to constitute a Committee for the purpose of recommending 
amendments to the Constitution byway of adding a new chapter on the governance of coalition 

Private Member's [23 NOV. 2007] Business Resolutions    155 
Governments providing for the powers, duties and responsibilities of coalition partners, and for 
providing a code of conduct in the matters where Co nstitutional provisions may not be 
practicable". 
Sir, in this country, there are nearly 150 registered and unregistered political parties, in some 
form or the other. Registration of political parties has also become quite easy these days because 
recognition can come in later, but parties can be registered with submission of their constitution, 
application, etc. Even such political parties get a common symbol by default. There is a procedure 
provided for this. Therefore, the number of political parties is increasing day in, day out, I must say, 
to spoil the political atmosphere in this country. Although they have got every right to form 
associations and groups, ultimately it leads to spoiling the political atmosphere in the country. We 
have got diverse culture and people of various castes, communities and religions are residing in 
this country. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH) in the Chair. 
A famous journalist has, therefore, said, "The real diversity of India often socially proclaimed 
is now becoming increasingly manifest politically. Coalition politics is the latest political 
manifestation of this impulse. Whatever, which is there in the country in general terms, has crept 
in into the poitical system of this country." 
There have been various attempts to form coalition Governments in this country. Some have 
been successful and some have been successful partly, if you look into the short history of political 
functioning in this country. The first attempt, as we all know, was made during 1977—80, when the 
Janata Party ruled for two-and-a-half years; it could not last more than two years for whatever may 
be the reasons. Then, Charan Singhji came as the next Prime Minister, and his Government lasted 
for about three weeks. In 1980, the Congress (I) go t an absolute majority and we ruled 
substantially. Again, in 1984—89, we completed the five years' term. Then, in 1989 elections, 
again a coalition Government headed by Shri V.P. Singh. It lasted for 11 months. Then came 
Chandra Sekharji, whose Government lasted for four months. Then, in 1990-91, Narasimha Raoji's 
Government, again a coalition Government, was a successful Government, in spite of all odds in 
between. Subsequently, in 1996, Vajpayeeji's Government was installed, which lasted for 13 days. 
Then, the Government led by Shri Deve Gowda lasted for one year. Gujralji's Government lasted 
for seven months. Then, in 1996, the NDA Government led by Vajpayeeji was a successful 
Government,— successful, not in the literal term—in the sense that it lasted for five years. Then, 
now the UPA Government is in power. The question is whether coalition Governments are beneficial 
for this country or not, that is a matter of opinio n. But one must admit that coalition 
Governments are a compulsion... 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Pondicherry): What is your opinon? 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: I am saying, from time to time, what happened. I would say 
that eventually. Let me summarise at the end. Sir, if we look at the system in the Constitutional 
provisions, coalition Governments become a compulsi on. No one can say that coalition 
Governments are good. If they are there by situation, by compulsion, then, we should see to it that 
they work out. As it is, let us not pray for coalition Governments. Nobody should pray for coalition 
Governments. But if it. comes as a result of the voting pattern, we have to function under that. That 
is why I say, they have crept in, and they are going to last for some more time to come. Now, why I 
am saying that some Constitutional provisions are required is that in the present system, when an 
election takes place, a party or a group of

of blackmailing is involved in this process. One ca nnot deny that. Even after giving letters,

or in the Rashtrapati Bhawan at the Central level. That concept came. Then came the concept

Therefore, one thing I feel is that whether you pro vide for Constitutional provisions or not, 
every aspect of our functioning should be in line with these provisions. Like, in the event of

right from voting till the scrutiny and counting of  votes. But, it states nothing about post-

I would like to touch Goa because Shri Pany wanted me to speak on it. In smaller States, 
the situation is the worst because there are Constituencies with just 25,000 votes BJP and

the courts and courts giving judgements. In Bihar case also, it happened. But it will keep on 
multiplying and multiplying. This is also not a very healthy situation where judiciary intervenes in 
the political process on top of the head. The large r principles are there. Now, the larger 
principles have come about. After the Bommai Judgement, any Central Government is finding it 
dificult to impose President's Rule. That is a good  decision. The principles have been laid 
down but the working of all these principles must be left in the hands of the political process. 
Sir, I am an eternal optimist man. I think that thi s whole process of uncertainty which is 
happening would give us a ray of hope for the futur e and the people of the country would 
revert to a stable polity where, maybe, two parties dominate and other regional parties would 
also become a very healthy, cooperative, compatriot on the national scene. This is a transitional

[SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD] 
phase. Why I say so, Sir? In conclusion, let me say one thing that the greatest speed of Indian 
economic progress has been witnessed when India is governed by coalition Governments, be it 
Mr. Vajpayee's Government or your Government. Yes, Left are Left. It may be that American 
capital losses its imperial colour when it gets invested in Kolkata. But, it is a problem in Delhi and

and reflect upon the kind of polity India is witnessing. Some parties are recognised State parties 
like TDP, RJD, Samajwadi Party, DMK and AIADMK. But, apart from the BJP and the Congress, 
the other political formultion claming to have pretence of national outlook was the CPM and CPI.

remember, I come from Bihar, CPI was the biggest opposition party after Congress in 50s and 60s. 
CPM was a big force in Andhra Pradesh and also in Maharashtra. They had a powerful presence in 
Tamil Nadu. They were very important in Punjab also. But, why is it that today CPM is confined to 
three States only, one is important, another is second and the rest is a very small North-Eastern 
State. Why? I think, the people of the country have a very basic instinct to understand which party is 
capable of being designated as a national party and which party is not. Therefore, by the very political 
process itself, the BJP and the Congress have emerg ed as all-India parties. A healthy 
competition; East Bengal and Mohan Bagan; Good! It is good for the development of the country.

you trust the entrepreneurial ability of the people of the country, they will give you regards. These 
developments offer me a great assurance of future, Sir, and I am quite sure, through the process of 
democracy, India is destined to become a world power economically, politically, militarily and also 
spiritually. Thank you, Sir for having given me time. 
PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Let me ask one doubt please. I am not opposing you. Are you saying

allow them to do their business properly, if you allow them to work in a convenient atmosphere, the 
Indian enterprise, the Indian intellect delivers with heart. That is what I am saying. 
DR. K. KESHAVA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Sir. I have heard Mr. Prasad and also the 
Mover of the Resolution. Sir, I have not come here with any studied notes. But, I would rather 
respond. Since you have tried to take the debate to the higher plain of discussion, let us first 
understand the society that we have inherited it is a stratified society, is a coalition society. We are a

Yet, we have been one, which perhaps my friends this side might oppose. What is that spirit that has 
Seen holding us together? If a society could be held together with these diversified social groups, 
why can't it be translated into politics? Since Mr. Prasad referred to the tall personality, Panditji, 
Congress itself is a coalition party. All things to all people. I could be an extreme left in the 
Congress with an extreme right man presiding over. I can understand that you are trying to rely 
more upon a political process and set democratic process to its tune. I want Mr. Prasad and others of 
his ilk to understand that very interpretation and functioning of democracy is undergone a lot of different 
interpretations. 

Private Member's [23 NOV. 2007] Business Resolutions    165 
First of all, democracy inherits clashes. Then, there is the inevitability of clash that is innate in 
democracy. Let us understand that first. If I am to prove that I have a majority over you and thus 
entitled for power. I have to go to the people, fight amongst ourselves and prove to people after a 
fight for one month — Or. Gill sahib would give us the rules that I have a majority. Next, nobody 
says, as he said, neither the Constitution says, how I should behave. He told me how I could come 
here. I can only come after using my lathi or my muscle or my money or my caste or my region or 
whatever it is to gain majority over my rival. This kind of a clash is inherent in democratic process, 
election Process. Then next process of democracy is how do I function in a House where the polity 
is controlled. Now that is what exactly the Mover of the Resolution was concerned with. While what 
you have said is true that the founding fathers of our Constitution had never envisaged, if not 
visioned, this kind of 200 parties coming into play and each one trying to compete with each 
other, and in this competition their eyes are glued was nothing but seat of power. The seat of power 
being the centre of attraction, all these issues which crop up need to be sorted out. I am not trying 
to immediately suggest that there has to be a change in the Constitution or bring an amendment to the 
Constitution. Nor the Mover of the Resolution said this. What he has said is that if there is a need 
for it. why not it be taken up. If the Constitution amendment is not helping us, can there be a code of 
conduct, to which you have referred? A code of conduct is nothing but a democractic process. Sir, 
how do we give shape to this democratic process is another issue which concerns all politicans. Sir, I 
was wondering whether in present globalised era, are we able to still talk about some kind of a 
complete sovereignty? Are we not to shed this sovereignty at all? Let us take climate changes. A 
partcular UN committee might come and ask you behave in such and such fashion. You give up 
your sovereignty. So, things are changing. Whether you accept them through the Constitution, or 
accept them through the debates, or accept them through changed rules, it is not the question here 
today. 
The democracy, about which Mr. Prasad talked firstly, the underpinning of such democracy should 
be that it should be responsive; it should be responsive to the needs of the time. If democractic 
process, or democracy as such, is not able to respond to the times, then it losses all its strength, 
meaning and content. That is what exactly the Mover of the Resolution has in view. And it is very 
imaginative of Mr. Naik to make this House exercise its mind over the tilings that are coming to. This 
is what exactly we are trying to discuss today. We, all politicians, in a coalition era are short-term 
maximisers. We want to attain everything within a short time. And I totally agree that coalition is 
nobody's choice. If everybody wants to give me full power, I will enjoy it. But things are not so. What 
is required therefore in this age when coalition has becomes compulsion is that we develop what Mr. 
Prasad referred to as, enduring traditions. Let me tell you that even the founding fathers did not 
depend too much on constitutional amendments. They depended on these conventions, if you 
were to read the Constitution between the lines and Understand its spirit, it is the founding fathers who 
always thought the evolution of democracy in this country would be through developing conventions. 
But the blurred conventions, which Mr. Naik has listed out, have failed us. So what is the answer? 
A day would certainly come when a healthy two party-coalition would be there. I understand that 
BJP and Congress Party, which are pan-Indian, will be there but others have to join them. I would 
certainly agree to it. But on what basis? Will it be on the pre-poll basis or will it be on the post-poll 
basis like the CMP that you would evolve? Whatever it is, what you take up will depend on how you 
respond to the people's needs. This, exactly, what the democracy has to do. Sir, Mr. Naik has 
referred to the Representation of the People's Act. It is true that it has done very good. It has got 
some kind of a democractic element into our 

166 Private Member's [RAJYA SABHA]                       Business Resolutions  
[SHRI K. KESHAVA RAO] 
Parliamentary system of governance. But, it has not bothered as to see who came in although 
it tried to see that the best man comes in. And, as is said, money plays a role at some places; 
muscle plays a role at some places. They could not be stopped that. They tried. But, you 
have your own methods of countering and overcoming them. This is what exactly is happening. 
That is another aspect which the Mover of the Resolution wanted to take note of. 
In the end, what is happening is, that, democracy is adjusting itself slowly. Sir, it is evoliving 
itself. We need to look into that. Sir, let us take  the Central Government of today or of the 
past, it encapsules the polity of coalitions in it, be it a one-party Government or a two-party 
Government or the coalition Government. That is how it really evolved itself. That has been 
our experience right from the beginning. It is not that coalitions have come only in 1970s. In 
1950-51 also, in Cochin and Travancore, we had them. In Andhra, in 1953, we had a coalition 
Government. In 1967, we had SVD Government. PEPSU had in 1951-52. Punjab had it. So, 
almost all the States in the country had coalition Governments and they ran well. But, that 
was based on traditions. But, the values have changed; techniques have changed; the needs 
of politicians have changed; the greed of the polit icians has changed. In that context, what 
do we do? If Avesta was to give everything, there w as no need for Hinduism to emerge. If 
Hinduism was an answer to all, there was no need fo r Taoism to come. If Taoism was an 
answer to all the ills of the society, there was no  need for Christianity if Christianity was an 
answer to all this, there was no need for Islam to come. If Islam was an answer, the Sikhism 
would not have come. Social philosophy tells us. Th at whenever there is some kind of a 
crisis in the society which transcends time and space, new philosphy emerge. That needs to 
be understood and tackled. In a polity, that exactly is the situation. After all, what is politics? 
Politics is nothing but a social order. You reflect  the social need. We always talk about 
politicians. At least, I know, when I went to a village and asked for a school, people branded 
me as a social worker. But, I did not get the school at that time. Then, I collected signatures 
of the people for it. People called me a public wor ker. When I did not get it and went on to 
become a Sarpanch to get a school, they called me a political worker. It is an evolution of a 
social worker into a political worker. That is what we say that all these politicians are trying to 
behave. But, there have to be some rules to the gam e. That is what the Mover of the 
Resolution wanted us to understand. We have examples to learn. We have many countries in 
Europe which have these coalitions. We have them in  Africa, in Latin America, etc. Only 
thing is we need to know how they functioning? At t he same time, if Gill Saheb were to be 
asked, he would say that they are not a healthy as they look from distance. The question 
today is: What is tickling us? I know your concern arose because although we join initially on 
a good tenor and tone, the moment we get into power , our own compulsions, our sectarian 
approaches and our own timely needs will make us use some kind of pressure or which you 
might call blackmail the other party or twist the a rm of the govt, to get things done. That 
exactly has made you concerned and unhappy. There are, for example, inter-State river water 
disputes, allocation of funds, devolution of  powers for the States etc. Paradoxically, what is 
happening is, every leader in the State wants coali tion at the Centre, but autonomy at the 
State. We don't want any interference from any quarter at the State level. At the same time, 
because the Centre has to run the Government, and only the Congress and the BJP can do it, 
they join one party or the other as a compulsion. So, they want the coalition at the Centre and 
autonomy in the State. This is our political psyche of evolving democracy. In such a situation, 
something must come in. As 5 told you about the religion, the Constitution is another bigger 
religion, so some kind of a rule, which needs constant monitoring. I am not trying to say that

there should be some kind of a constitutional amend ment. Even if it is coming, let it come. 
There is nothing wrong in it. But even as a voice, what kind of an understanding you would 
enter into although I am not trying to talk about MoUs that it talks about, and of which stamp 
paper MoUs you are talking about. When you can talk about black magic in a State changing

talk, is a country where you have not seen 7 per cent of people who live a in places which are

Mere talking would not help. This is a society wher e touching another human being was a 
crime under some kind of a dharma. We need to take all these things into consideration, 
while fighting them.
